evidence_quotes.quote: This paper investigates the interplay between HWA and emerging water-sharing regimes in the IHR, focusing on their inclusion and exclusion within state policy-frameworks.

This study initially employs a textual analysis of policy documents to look for HWA recognition and integration information. PHIM has been devised as a primary analytical tool to evaluate the case studies.
On-ground action also included removal of encroachments at some sites, ongoing desilting and creating protective zones around the naulas to enhance recharge capacity (Tewari 2018).
yet the absence of comprehensive research studies keeps evaluation of critical metrics like equity, cost-effectiveness and adaptive capacity limited to conceptual.

criterion_notes.c1: Discusses community domestic water access in the Indian Himalayan Region (Uttarakhand) through traditional spring-fed Heritage Water Architecture (naulaas, dharas, guls) alongside piped water infrastructure, although two of the three illustrative cases focus primarily on urban river rejuvenation (Rispana River) and watershed recharge structures (chal-khols).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2 because it examines national and state water policy frameworks, multi-tiered water governance, and inter-agency institutional fragmentation in Uttarakhand. However, it FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 because it examines macro-level policy recognition of traditional water structures and generic conservation/restoration project delivery (spring desilting, riverbed afforestation, watershed recharge) rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Note that plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude because the paper independently fails Criteria 3, 4, and 5.
criterion_notes.c3: Presents a conceptual typology (the Policy-Heritage Integration Matrix, PHIM) supported by a high-level textual overview of eight national/state policy documents and three brief narrative case vignettes synthesized from secondary literature, NGO reports, and newspaper articles. It collects no primary empirical data, reports no systematic empirical synthesis methodology, and explicitly notes in the Conclusion that the absence of comprehensive research studies keeps evaluation of critical metrics like equity limited to conceptual.
criterion_notes.c4: Categorizes projects into PHIM quadrants (e.g., synergistic coexistence, tokenistic inclusion, functional appropriation) and cites physical conservation implementation outputs from secondary sources (such as naula desilting, water-quality testing, and 30% riverbank afforestation completion), rather than empirically measuring household or community water access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: No primary household, individual, or community sample or measured service-access outcome is identifiable; the unit of discussion consists of macro policy documents and secondary project-level restoration summaries.

study_design: Conceptual policy analysis and secondary narrative case overview
population_and_sample: Eight national/state water policy documents (2002-2023) and three secondary municipal/district project vignettes in Uttarakhand (Almora, Dehradun, and Pithoragarh); no primary household or community sample reported
exposure: Policy recognition and institutional integration of Heritage Water Architecture (naulaas, dharas, chal-khols) and river/watershed restoration initiatives across state and national water policies
outcome: Policy-Heritage Integration Matrix (PHIM) classification of policy recognition and project-level ecological/physical restoration implementation (e.g., naula desilting, riverbank afforestation completion); no household or community service access outcome measured
rationale: Excluded (E05): This article is a policy-design overview and conceptual framework paper proposing the Policy-Heritage Integration Matrix (PHIM) using a high-level summary of eight policy documents and three brief secondary vignettes from published literature and media reports in Uttarakhand, with no primary empirical data and no systematic empirical synthesis (explicitly stating that evaluation of equity and adaptive capacity remains limited to conceptual). In addition, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (examining macro-policy heritage recognition and conservation/river-rejuvenation project implementation rather than rule-type mechanisms governing service access) and reports physical restoration outputs rather than household or community water service access outcomes (failing Criteria 4 and 5, so plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude).
